title: Japanese Nutmeg-yew: Ancient Nutmeg-yew Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: Kaya, a slow evergreen conifer and the wood of go boards. The Great Kaya of Yokomuro in Maebashi, one of Japan's three great kaya, is 8.1 metres round.
intro: Torreya nucifera, called kaya in Japan, is a slow evergreen conifer that looks the same in February as in August, which is part of why its oldest specimens went unnoticed for centuries; its wood is what every serious go player wants a board cut from. Japan names three great kaya trees. The one at Yokomuro in Maebashi earns its place on girth, 8.1 metres round, and the one at Kitahama stands alone behind a white fence on farmland near Hamamatsu, viewed from the road. Yono no Okaya in Saitama City is traditionally dated to the 1030s. The kaya at Nagoya Castle carries a stranger claim: the first Owari lord ate its nuts before marching on Osaka in 1615, and his successors kept eating them every New Year after. None gives up its age easily; surveys and temple tradition disagree, sometimes by centuries.
